response.content:
All three child proposals were submitted but returned no results from the controller, so I'll synthesize the full brief directly.

# Technical Brief: Distributed Consensus and Coordination

## 1. Raft

Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety. Three mechanisms deserve detailed treatment.

**Leader election with randomized timeouts.** Time is divided into monotonically increasing *terms*. A follower that hears no AppendEntries heartbeat within its election timeout transitions to candidate, increments its current term, votes for itself, and issues RequestVote RPCs. A candidate wins by collecting votes from a majority quorum; each server grants at most one vote per term (persisted to stable storage before replying), which guarantees at most one leader per term — the Election Safety property. Randomized timeouts (e.g., 150–300 ms) break symmetry and make split votes rare. The *voting restriction* in RequestVote is the safety-critical piece: a voter rejects any candidate whose log is not at least as up-to-date as its own, where up-to-dateness is compared first by last log term, then by log length. This enforces the Leader Completeness property — every elected leader contains all committed entries — so Raft never needs to "catch up" a new leader as Viewstamped Replication does during view change. The PreVote extension has a would-be candidate poll peers without incrementing its term, preventing a partitioned node from disrupting a stable leader when it rejoins with an inflated term.

**Log replication and the Log Matching property.** The leader appends client commands to its log and replicates via AppendEntries, which carries prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm as a consistency check. Followers reject the RPC if their entry at prevLogIndex does not match that term; the leader then decrements nextIndex for that follower and retries, forcing divergent follower suffixes to be overwritten with the leader's log. This maintains the Log Matching invariant: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical through that index. An entry is *committed* when the leader has replicated it on a majority *and* the entry is from the leader's current term — the latter restriction (§5.4.2 of Ongaro–Ousterhout) prevents the famous counterexample in which a leader counts replicas of an old-term entry and that entry is later overwritten. Committed entries are applied in order to the state machine (the applied index trails the commit index), giving replicated state machine semantics.

**Linearizable reads via ReadIndex and leader leases.** Naively serving reads from the leader is unsafe because a deposed leader may not know it has been replaced. The ReadIndex optimization has the leader record its current commit index, confirm leadership with a round of heartbeats to a majority, wait for its applied index to reach the recorded commit index, then serve the read — linearizable without writing a log entry. The lease-based variant lets the leader serve reads without the heartbeat round for the duration of a lease measured from the last successful quorum round-trip, assuming bounded clock drift; this trades a timing assumption for latency. Leadership transfer (TimeoutNow) lets an operator or load balancer move the leader gracefully: the old leader brings the target fully up to date, then instructs it to start an immediate election.

## 2. Paxos

**Single-decree (Basic) Paxos.** Roles are proposers, acceptors, and learners. Phase 1a: a proposer selects a proposal number *n* (totally ordered, unique per proposer) and sends Prepare(n). Phase 1b: an acceptor that has not promised a higher number responds with a promise never to accept proposals numbered below *n*, attaching the highest-numbered proposal it has already accepted, if any. Phase 2a: upon promises from a majority, the proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v must be the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported in phase 1b, or the proposer's own value if none was reported — this is the *value selection rule* that guarantees agreement. Phase 2b: acceptors accept unless they have promised a higher number. A value is *chosen* once accepted by a majority; majorities pairwise intersect, so any later proposer's phase 1 quorum contains at least one acceptor that saw the chosen value, forcing the proposer to re-propose it. Safety holds under asynchrony; liveness requires a distinguished proposer (a leader elected by, e.g., an Ω failure detector), because dueling proposers can livelock by repeatedly preempting each other's prepares — exactly the scenario FLP says cannot be deterministically avoided.

**Multi-Paxos.** Running full Basic Paxos per log slot costs two round trips per command. Multi-Paxos amortizes phase 1: a stable leader runs Prepare once over an infinite suffix of instances, then commits each subsequent command with a single phase-2 round (one round trip plus learner notification). This is what production systems (Chubby's Paxos, Spanner's per-group Paxos) actually run. Practical issues Lamport's paper leaves open — log holes, state transfer to lagging replicas, leader election, and reconfiguration — are what papers like "Paxos Made Live" (Chandra, Griesemer, Redstone) document: disk corruption handling, snapshots coordinated with the log, and the use of a master lease so the leader can serve local reads.

**Flexible Paxos and EPaxos.** Flexible Paxos (Howard, Malkhi, Spiegelman) proves that Paxos does not require majority quorums; it requires only that every phase-1 quorum intersect every phase-2 quorum (|Q1| + |Q2| > N for simple quorums). Since phase 2 is the steady-state cost, one can shrink Q2 (fast replication) at the price of a larger Q1 (slower, rarer leader election) — grid quorums make this concrete. Egalitarian Paxos (EPaxos) eliminates the distinguished leader entirely: any replica proposes; commands that do not interfere commit in one round trip on a fast-path quorum (⌈3N/4⌉-ish, precisely F + ⌊(F+1)/2⌋ beyond the command leader for N = 2F+1), while interfering commands record dependencies and are ordered by a deterministic topological sort of the resulting dependency graph at execution time. This yields optimal commit latency in the wide area and load balancing, at the cost of significantly more complex execution and recovery logic.

## 3. Lease-Based Coordination

**Gray–Cheriton leases.** The original 1989 formulation: a lease is a time-bounded grant of authority (originally, cache-consistency authority) that a server issues to a client. Correctness rests on a bounded clock-drift assumption rather than synchronized clocks: the grantor starts its timer when it *sends* the lease and the holder when it *receives* it, so the holder's view of expiry is conservatively shorter. If the holder crashes or partitions, the grantor merely waits out the lease before reassigning — no agreement protocol needed on the failure path. The fundamental tradeoff is availability versus recovery time: long leases reduce renewal traffic but lengthen the unavailability window after a holder failure.

**Chubby locks and sequencers.** Google's Chubby is a Paxos-replicated lock service exporting coarse-grained advisory locks with session semantics: a client maintains a session via KeepAlives; if the session lease expires the client's locks are released. Because a lock holder may be paused (GC, VM stall) and act after its lease has expired, Chubby introduces *sequencers*: an opaque, monotonically increasing token describing the lock generation, which the holder passes to downstream services; those services validate the sequencer against Chubby (or reject lower generations), converting the lock into a fencing mechanism. Chubby also supports lock-delay for servers that cannot check sequencers. This is the canonical answer to the "stale lock holder" problem that pure mutual-exclusion-by-lease cannot solve.

**ZooKeeper sessions and ephemeral nodes.** ZooKeeper implements leases implicitly: a client session has a timeout negotiated with the ensemble; *ephemeral znodes* created by the session are deleted automatically when the session expires, which is the primitive underlying leader election recipes (lowest sequential ephemeral node under an election path wins; watchers on the predecessor avoid herd effects). Safety again requires fencing: ZooKeeper's zxid or a monotonic epoch counter stored in a znode serves as the fencing token, and downstream resources must reject operations bearing stale tokens — Kleppmann's critique of Redlock is essentially that a lease without an externally checked fencing token cannot provide mutual exclusion under process pauses.

**Clock-bound leader leases in Spanner.** Spanner's Paxos leaders hold ~10 s leases whose disjointness is enforced using TrueTime: a leader only considers its lease valid until TT.now().earliest exceeds the lease end as computed from votes, and a successor waits out the uncertainty interval, guaranteeing that leader lease intervals for a Paxos group are disjoint in real time. This is what makes local, lock-free linearizable reads at the leader safe, and what lets commit timestamps respect external consistency (commit-wait).

## 4. Membership Changes

**Raft joint consensus.** To move from configuration C_old to C_new, the leader first replicates a special entry C_old,new; once appended (not committed), servers use the joint configuration, in which both election and commitment require *separate* majorities of C_old and of C_new. After C_old,new commits, the leader replicates C_new, after which C_old majorities are irrelevant. The two-phase structure guarantees that at no instant can disjoint majorities of C_old and C_new both make unilateral decisions, eliminating the window in which two leaders for different configurations could both commit.

**Raft single-server changes and the 2015 bug.** The dissertation's simpler scheme restricts each change to adding or removing one server, since any majority of the old configuration and any majority of the new one necessarily intersect when they differ by one member. Ongaro's 2015 correction: a new configuration entry may only be appended after the leader has committed an entry in its *current term*, because otherwise two concurrent single-server changes starting from different (uncommitted) base configurations can produce non-intersecting quorums and elect two leaders. Implementations (etcd historically, TiKV) also diverge on when a configuration takes effect — at append versus at commit — with append-time application being the provably safe choice in the original design. A further operational mechanism is the *learner/non-voting* stage: a new server replicates the log without quorum rights until caught up, preventing availability loss while it snapshots.

**Reconfiguration in the Paxos/VR family.** Lamport's approach treats the configuration as state machine state: the configuration used for instance *i* is the one determined by instance *i − α*, where α bounds pipeline concurrency; setting α = 1 serializes, larger α allows pipelining at the cost of delayed reconfiguration effect. "Stoppable Paxos" / Vertical Paxos instead ends the old configuration with an explicit stop command and starts a new log, with an external (auxiliary) master blessing configurations — this is closer to how Chubby and Spanner move replicas. Viewstamped Replication Revisited (Liskov–Cowling) separates *view changes* (same membership, new primary: DoViewChange messages carry logs; the new primary adopts the longest, most recent log, giving the completeness Raft gets from its voting rule) from *reconfiguration*, which runs through the normal case as a special request, wedges the old group at a reconfiguration point, and transfers state to the new epoch's members before they begin.

## 5. Consistency Models

**Linearizability.** The gold standard for single-object consistency (Herlihy–Wing): every operation appears to take effect atomically at some point between its invocation and response, and the resulting total order respects real time — if op A completes before op B begins, A precedes B. It is *composable* (local): a system of linearizable objects is linearizable, unlike sequential consistency. It is what "CP" in CAP means by consistency, what Raft/Paxos replicated state machines provide for writes, and what ReadIndex/lease reads preserve for reads. Checking it is NP-complete in general (hence tools like Jepsen's Knossos/Porcupine use heuristic search).

**Sequential and causal consistency.** Sequential consistency (Lamport) requires a single total order consistent with each process's program order, but *not* with real time — a process may read arbitrarily stale data as long as everyone agrees on one history. Causal consistency requires only that operations related by potential causality (Lamport's happens-before: program order plus reads-from) be observed in order everywhere; concurrent writes may be seen in different orders by different replicas. Causal+ (as in COPS) adds convergent conflict handling so replicas eventually agree on concurrent-write outcomes. The practically important theorem (Mahajan et al.; Attiya et al.) is that real-time causal consistency is the strongest model achievable in an always-available, partition-tolerant ("AP") convergent system.

**Session guarantees and eventual consistency.** The Bayou session guarantees — read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads — give per-client sanity without global ordering; jointly they imply a form of causal consistency per session. Eventual consistency promises only convergence in the absence of new updates; making it principled requires convergent merge, which is what CRDTs provide: state-based CRDTs (CvRDTs) require state to form a join-semilattice with merge = least upper bound (G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set with add-wins semantics via unique tags), while op-based CRDTs (CmRDTs) require commutative concurrent operations over a causal delivery channel. Finally, Spanner's *external consistency* is linearizability at whole-database, multi-operation granularity: TrueTime commit-wait ensures that if T1 commits before T2 starts, T1's timestamp is smaller, so snapshot reads at a timestamp observe a real-time-consistent prefix.

## 6. Failure Modes

**Crash-stop, crash-recovery, and the role of stable storage.** Protocol correctness proofs are parameterized by failure model. Crash-recovery (the realistic model) obligates specific persistence points: a Raft server must fsync currentTerm, votedFor, and log entries before acknowledging RPCs; a Paxos acceptor must persist its promised and accepted values before replying. Violating these — e.g., acknowledging before fsync, or losing data to disk-level corruption — silently converts a crash fault into something worse. "Paxos Made Live" describes checksumming and a mode where a replica with a corrupted disk rejoins as a non-voting learner until it has observed a full instance window, so it can never falsely deny a past promise. Related: fsync failure semantics (the PostgreSQL "fsyncgate" class of bugs) mean a failed fsync may leave page cache marked clean, so retrying is unsound — protocols must treat fsync failure as a crash.

**Network partitions and split-brain.** Quorum intersection is the generic defense: a minority partition in Raft/Multi-Paxos can elect no leader and commit nothing, so at most one side makes progress. Split-brain arises when systems substitute timeouts plus non-intersecting authority for quorums: the classic primary/backup with a replication link failure, or a lease holder paused past expiry acting without a fencing check. Asymmetric and partial partitions produce subtler livelocks: a node that can send but not receive (or can reach the leader but not other followers) can, in pre-PreVote Raft, repeatedly trigger elections and depose a healthy leader (term inflation); CheckQuorum (leader steps down if it cannot heartbeat a majority) handles the dual case where the leader is isolated from followers but clients can still reach it, which otherwise breaks lease reads.

**Byzantine faults and gray failures.** Byzantine faults allow arbitrary, including adversarial, behavior. PBFT (Castro–Liskov) tolerates f Byzantine replicas with N = 3f+1 using three phases (pre-prepare, prepare, commit) with quorums of 2f+1, MACs/signatures, and view changes carrying certified prepared sets; the 2f+1 quorum size ensures any two quorums intersect in at least f+1 replicas, hence at least one honest one. Distinct from Byzantine behavior are *gray failures* (Huang et al.) and *fail-slow* hardware: a component that passes health checks but performs orders of magnitude below spec (a NIC dropping 1% of packets, a disk with 100× latency) — differential observability between the detector and the clients is the defining feature, and it degrades consensus systems (a fail-slow Raft leader stalls the whole group without triggering election timeouts). Clock-related failures form a third class: leader leases and TrueTime both assume bounded drift; a frequency error beyond the assumed bound (or an NTP step) can make "disjoint" leases overlap, which is why Spanner treats clock uncertainty as a first-class, measured quantity and evicts machines with misbehaving oscillators.

## 7. Atomic Broadcast

Atomic (total-order) broadcast requires validity, uniform agreement, integrity, and *total order*: all correct processes deliver the same messages in the same order. The foundational result (Chandra–Toueg) is that atomic broadcast and consensus are equivalent — each is implementable from the other — so every impossibility and quorum bound for consensus transfers.

**Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast).** Zab orders state changes with zxids, 64-bit pairs ⟨epoch, counter⟩. Protocol phases: discovery (prospective leader learns the latest epoch and most up-to-date history from a quorum), synchronization (leader brings followers' logs to a common prefix before any new proposal — this is where Zab differs most visibly from Raft, which repairs followers lazily during normal operation), and broadcast (two-phase: leader proposes, quorum of followers ACK, leader commits), with FIFO ordering guaranteed per leader by TCP channels. Zab's distinguishing requirement over generic atomic broadcast is *primary order*: because ZooKeeper replicates incremental (delta) state changes rather than idempotent commands, a prefix of a failed leader's proposals must never be reordered or interleaved with a new leader's — the epoch in the zxid plus synchronization enforces this.

**Viewstamped Replication.** VR (Oki–Liskov 1988, revisited 2012) is a primary-backup atomic broadcast/consensus protocol contemporaneous with Paxos. Normal case: the primary of the current *view* assigns op-numbers, sends Prepare, backups append in order and send PrepareOK, and the primary commits on f ACKs (quorum of f+1 of 2f+1 including itself), piggybacking commit-numbers. On suspected primary failure, replicas run a *view change*: StartViewChange messages gather a quorum, DoViewChange messages carry each replica's log with its last normal view, and the new primary (deterministically round-robin by view number) adopts the log from the highest ⟨last-normal-view, op-number⟩, then issues StartView. Correctness argument: any committed op is in f+1 logs, and the view-change quorum intersects that set, so the maximal adopted log contains all committed ops. VR Revisited adds recovery (a rebooting replica rejoins via a nonce-protected state transfer rather than relying on stable storage) and the reconfiguration protocol noted above.

**Virtual synchrony and group communication.** The ISIS toolkit (Birman–Joseph) introduced virtually synchronous process groups: membership changes are delivered as *view* events totally ordered relative to messages, and messages are delivered in the same view to all surviving members, so a multicast appears to happen "between" the same two views everywhere. Ordering layers range from FIFO (cbcast's causal order via vector timestamps) to abcast (total order, via a token or sequencer). This model underlies Spread, JGroups, and conceptually modern membership services. A fourth practical instance: Kafka's replication (ISR-based, and since KIP-500, KRaft — a Raft-derived metadata quorum) implements a totally ordered partition log, illustrating the "consensus = shared log" equivalence that systems like Corfu make explicit with a sequencer plus chained storage.

## 8. Impossibility Results

**FLP.** Fischer–Lynch–Paterson (1985): in an asynchronous system (no bounds on message delay or relative process speed), no *deterministic* protocol solves consensus if even one process may crash. The proof shows an initial bivalent configuration exists and that from any bivalent configuration an adversarial scheduler can always reach another bivalent configuration, constructing an infinite non-deciding run; the crux is that the "deciding step" can always be delayed by scheduling around a single critical process. FLP is a liveness impossibility — safety is achievable — and the escape hatches each relax one hypothesis: partial synchrony (Dwork–Lynch–Stockmeyer: consensus solvable once Global Stabilization Time is reached, which is the model Raft, Multi-Paxos, and PBFT actually inhabit), randomization (Ben-Or's protocol terminates with probability 1), and unreliable failure detectors. Chandra–Hadzilacos–Toueg proved Ω (eventual leader, equivalently ⋄W) is the *weakest* failure detector for consensus with a majority of correct processes — the theoretical justification for every leader-based protocol's structure.

**CAP and PACELC.** Gilbert–Lynch's formalization of Brewer's conjecture: no read/write register protocol can guarantee linearizability (C), availability of every operation at every non-failed node (A), and tolerance of arbitrary network partitions (P) simultaneously; during a partition, some node must either refuse service or return a non-linearizable result. Precision matters: P is not a "choice" (partitions happen), availability in the theorem is total node-level availability (quorum systems are "unavailable" in this strict sense on the minority side only), and C is linearizability specifically — weaker models like causal escape the theorem, which is exactly the content of the "strongest AP-achievable model" results cited in §5. PACELC (Abadi) extends the taxonomy: under Partition, trade A vs C; Else, trade Latency vs Consistency — capturing why Spanner (PC/EC) pays commit-wait latency while Dynamo-style systems (PA/EL) do not even absent partitions.

**Resilience bounds and the Two Generals problem.** For Byzantine agreement, Pease–Shostak–Lamport proved N ≥ 3f+1 is necessary (and sufficient) without message authentication in partial synchrony/synchrony-without-signatures settings; the classic N = 3, f = 1 scenario shows an honest process cannot distinguish which of two others is lying. Dwork–Lynch–Stockmeyer showed 3f+1 remains the bound for partially synchronous Byzantine consensus even *with* signatures, which is why PBFT and modern BFT (HotStuff, Tendermint) all use 3f+1 / quorums of 2f+1. Crash-fault consensus under partial synchrony needs N ≥ 2f+1 (majority quorums). The Two Generals problem (Gray's framing) proves no protocol achieves *common knowledge* of agreement over an unreliable link in finitely many messages — the reason distributed commit uses timeouts, retries, and idempotence rather than certainty. Finally, the Attiya–Welch lower bounds quantify the latency cost of strong consistency: with message uncertainty, linearizable reads or writes cannot all be local — worst-case operation latency is Ω(message delay) (read + write latency bounded below by u/2 terms) — whereas sequential consistency admits one-sided fast operations; this is the theoretical floor under every "strong consistency costs a round trip" engineering observation.

## Synthesis

The field's architecture follows from its impossibilities: FLP forces timing assumptions or randomness, which protocols package as failure detectors or election timeouts; quorum intersection (2f+1 crash, 3f+1 Byzantine, generalized by Flexible Paxos) is the universal safety mechanism; atomic broadcast's equivalence to consensus makes the replicated log (Raft, Multi-Paxos, Zab, VR) the dominant implementation idiom; leases convert timing assumptions into local-read performance but demand fencing to remain safe; membership change is consensus about the consensus group itself and is where the subtlest bugs live; and the consistency-model hierarchy, pinned at the top by linearizability and bounded below by CAP and Attiya–Welch, defines exactly what each system buys with the latency it spends.

Answer: The rigorous technical brief above covers all eight required areas — Raft (randomized leader election with the up-to-date voting restriction, log replication with the Log Matching/Leader Completeness properties and current-term commit rule, ReadIndex/lease reads plus PreVote and leadership transfer), Paxos (single-decree phases 1a/1b/2a/2b with the value-selection rule, Multi-Paxos amortized phase 1, Flexible Paxos quorum-intersection generalization and EPaxos dependency-ordered fast paths), lease-based coordination (Gray–Cheriton drift-bounded leases, Chubby sessions/sequencers as fencing tokens, ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes, Spanner TrueTime-disjoint leader leases), membership changes (Raft joint consensus C_old,new, the corrected single-server change rule with learners, Lamport α-window/stoppable-Paxos reconfiguration and VR view-change-vs-reconfiguration), consistency models (linearizability, sequential, causal/causal+, session guarantees, CRDTs, Spanner external consistency), failure modes (crash-recovery persistence obligations and fsync semantics, partitions/split-brain/asymmetric-partition livelock with PreVote/CheckQuorum, Byzantine faults via PBFT, gray/fail-slow failures, clock-drift lease violations), atomic broadcast (Zab with primary order and zxids, Viewstamped Replication view changes, virtual synchrony/ISIS, and the Chandra–Toueg consensus equivalence), and impossibility results (FLP with its bivalence proof and escape hatches, Ω/⋄W as the weakest failure detector, CAP/PACELC precisely stated, the 3f+1 Byzantine bound, Two Generals, and Attiya–Welch latency lower bounds).

# Consensus Protocols: Raft, the Paxos Family, and Atomic Broadcast

## 1. Raft

Raft (Ongaro & Ousterhout, 2014) is a leader-based consensus protocol for replicated state machines over a crash-recovery model with 2f+1 servers tolerating f failures. It decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety, and uses **terms** — monotonically increasing integers acting as a logical clock — to detect stale information. Each term begins with an election and contains at most one leader; every RPC carries the sender's currentTerm, and any server receiving a higher term immediately updates its own and reverts to follower, while messages carrying a lower term are rejected. The persistent state on each server is currentTerm, votedFor, and the log itself.

**Leader election.** Servers are followers until an election timeout (randomized, e.g., 150–300 ms, to break symmetry and avoid repeated split votes) expires without hearing a valid AppendEntries heartbeat from the current leader. The follower becomes a candidate: it increments currentTerm, votes for itself, and issues RequestVote RPCs carrying its lastLogIndex and lastLogTerm. A voter grants its vote only if it has not voted for another candidate in this term (votedFor is persisted to survive crashes) and the candidate's log is at least as **up-to-date**: the candidate's last entry has a higher term, or the same term and at least equal index. A candidate winning a majority becomes leader; if the vote splits, candidates time out again with fresh randomized timeouts.

**Log replication.** The leader appends client commands to its log and replicates them via AppendEntries RPCs, which carry prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm as a consistency check: a follower rejects the RPC unless its log contains an entry at prevLogIndex with matching term; on conflict, the follower truncates its suffix and accepts the leader's entries. The leader maintains nextIndex and matchIndex per follower, decrementing nextIndex (or using a conflict-term fast-backup optimization) until the check passes, which makes follower logs converge to the leader's. The **commitIndex** advances when an entry is stored on a majority — with the crucial restriction that a leader only counts replicas for entries of its *own current term* (this closes the "Figure 8" anomaly where an old-term entry replicated to a majority could still be overwritten); earlier entries are then committed transitively. Followers learn the commit index via the leaderCommit field and apply entries up to it (tracked by lastApplied). A newly elected leader therefore typically commits a **no-op entry** in its term to learn the current commit frontier.

**Safety properties.** The **Log Matching Property** states that if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical in all entries up through that index; it follows inductively from the fact that a leader creates at most one entry per index per term and from the AppendEntries consistency check. The **Leader Completeness Property** states that if an entry is committed in term T, it is present in the log of the leader of every term greater than T; it is guaranteed by the up-to-date voting restriction, since a candidate cannot win without the votes of a majority that intersects the majority holding the committed entry. Together these yield the State Machine Safety property: all servers apply the same command at each log index.

**Membership change.** The original mechanism is **joint consensus**: the leader appends a configuration entry C(old,new) under which agreement (for both elections and commitment) requires *separate majorities of both* the old and new configurations; once C(old,new) is committed, the leader appends C(new), after which the old configuration is irrelevant. Configuration entries take effect when appended, not when committed. The simpler and now more common alternative is **single-server membership change**: adding or removing one server at a time guarantees that any old-configuration majority and new-configuration majority intersect, so no joint phase is needed. Two refinements matter in practice: new servers should first join as non-voting learners and catch up before counting toward quorums, and (per Ongaro's post-dissertation correction) a new leader must commit an entry in its own term before admitting a further configuration change, otherwise two interleaved single-server changes can produce disjoint quorums. A leader removed from the configuration steps down after committing C(new).

**PreVote and check-quorum.** A partitioned server repeatedly timing out inflates its term and, upon rejoining, forces the legitimate leader to step down. The **PreVote** phase has the would-be candidate ask peers whether they *would* grant a vote, without incrementing any term; only on a majority of positive pre-votes does it start a real election. This is usually paired with leader "stickiness" (a server rejects RequestVote if it heard from a live leader within the minimum election timeout) and check-quorum (a leader steps down if it cannot reach a majority), which together also protect lease-based reads.

**Leadership transfer.** For planned handoff, the leader stops accepting new proposals, replicates until the target's log is fully caught up, then sends a TimeoutNow RPC; the target immediately starts an election in the next term, bypassing PreVote and stickiness, and wins because its log is current. A timeout aborts the transfer and the old leader resumes.

**ReadIndex and lease reads.** Linearizable reads need not be appended to the log. With **ReadIndex**, the leader records its current commitIndex as the readIndex, confirms it is still leader by exchanging heartbeats with a majority, waits until lastApplied ≥ readIndex, and then serves the read from local state; followers can serve reads by requesting a readIndex from the leader and waiting to apply up to it. A new leader must first commit its no-op before serving ReadIndex reads, since it does not otherwise know the commit frontier. **Lease reads** drop the heartbeat round: the leader serves reads locally during a lease window derived from the election timeout and a bounded clock-drift assumption (the lease starts at the time the heartbeat quorum round was initiated). This is cheaper but conditionally safe — it trades the asynchronous-model guarantee for a timing assumption.

## 2. The Paxos Family

**Single-decree (Basic) Paxos** (Lamport) chooses one value among proposers, acceptors, and learners, tolerating f crash failures with 2f+1 acceptors. Proposal numbers (ballots) are unique and totally ordered, typically (round, proposerID). In **Phase 1a (Prepare)** a proposer sends Prepare(n) to a quorum of acceptors. In **Phase 1b (Promise)**, an acceptor that has not already promised a number ≥ n responds with a promise never to accept any proposal numbered < n, including the highest-numbered proposal (n_a, v_a) it has already accepted, if any. In **Phase 2a (Accept)**, upon promises from a majority, the proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v must be the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported in the promises, or a free choice if none was reported — this is the P2c invariant that makes already-possibly-chosen values stick. In **Phase 2b (Accepted)**, an acceptor accepts (n, v) unless it has promised a higher number, and notifies learners. A value is **chosen** once a majority accepts it with the same ballot; quorum intersection guarantees any later Phase 1 sees it. Acceptors persist promised and accepted state. Safety holds under full asynchrony; liveness does not (consistent with FLP): dueling proposers can livelock, which is why implementations elect a distinguished proposer and use randomized backoff.

**Multi-Paxos** amortizes Phase 1 across a sequence of instances (log slots): a stable leader runs Prepare once with a ballot covering all instances, collecting per-slot accepted values, then runs only Phase 2 per client command — one round trip to a majority in steady state, structurally equivalent to Raft's AppendEntries. Leader election *is* the Prepare phase under this view. Gaps left by a failed leader are filled by proposing no-ops so execution can proceed in slot order; a stable-leader lease plus heartbeats provides the practical liveness Raft gets from election timeouts.

**Flexible Paxos (FPaxos)** (Howard, Malkhi, Spiegelman, 2016) observes that safety requires only that every Phase-1 quorum Q1 intersect every Phase-2 quorum Q2; two Phase-2 quorums need *not* intersect each other. With simple counting quorums this relaxes the majority rule to |Q1| + |Q2| > N, so a 5-node cluster may replicate to any 2 nodes (Q2) provided elections contact 4 (Q1). Grid quorums (Q1 = a row, Q2 = a column) are another instantiation. The trade is cheap, highly available steady-state replication against more expensive and less fault-tolerant recovery — attractive because Phase 2 runs per command while Phase 1 runs only per leader change. The same observation underlies Raft variants with asymmetric quorums.

**EPaxos (Egalitarian Paxos)** (Moraru, Andersen, Kaminsky, 2013) is leaderless: any replica acts as command leader for the commands it receives, removing the single-leader bottleneck and WAN detour. Each command is proposed with **dependencies** (interfering commands seen so far) and a **sequence number**. On the **fast path**, if a fast quorum — ⌊3N/4⌋-sized, more precisely F + ⌊(F+1)/2⌋ among N = 2F+1 — returns identical dependency sets, the command commits in one round trip. Otherwise the **slow path** runs a Paxos-Accept round on the union of reported dependencies. Execution is decoupled from commitment: replicas build the dependency graph, find strongly connected components, and execute them in topological order, breaking ties within an SCC by sequence number. Non-conflicting commands thus commit with optimal WAN latency; the costs are dependency-tracking complexity and degraded behavior under high conflict rates (and a subtle correctness bug in the original dependency-computation later identified and fixed in follow-up work).

**Cheap Paxos** (Lamport & Massa) runs steady state on F+1 main acceptors, keeping F **auxiliary acceptors** idle; auxiliaries participate only transiently during main-acceptor failure to restore quorums and help reconfigure, giving 2F+1-level tolerance at roughly F+1 cost (with weaker liveness: all F+1 main processors must be up for progress). **Vertical Paxos** (Lamport, Malkhi, Zhou) delegates reconfiguration to an auxiliary configuration master and lets quorums change per ballot ("vertically"), with distinct read and write quorums; it is notable for showing primary-backup replication (f+1 replicas tolerating f failures) as a special case of Paxos, and it is a theoretical ancestor of reconfigurable systems in the VR/Zab mold.

## 3. Atomic Broadcast

**Total-order broadcast equivalence.** Atomic (total-order) broadcast requires validity, (uniform) agreement, integrity, and total order: all correct processes deliver the same messages in the same order. Chandra and Toueg proved it is **equivalent to consensus** in asynchronous crash-failure systems: a sequence of consensus instances, each agreeing on the next batch of messages to deliver, implements TOB; conversely, TOB solves consensus by broadcasting proposals and deciding on the first delivered. Hence both inherit FLP impossibility and require the same failure-detector strength (Ω / ◊S) for solvability — Multi-Paxos, Raft, Zab, and VR are all, at bottom, total-order broadcast engines.

**Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast).** Zab drives ZooKeeper's replication across 2f+1 servers. Transactions are identified by a **zxid** = ⟨epoch, counter⟩, where the epoch increments with each new leader. The protocol runs in three phases: **discovery** (a prospective leader — chosen by fast leader election favoring the highest ⟨epoch, zxid⟩ — collects follower epochs and histories and establishes a new epoch), **synchronization** (the leader brings a quorum of followers consistent with its history via DIFF, TRUNC, or SNAP messages, after which it is established), and **broadcast** (a two-phase, pipelined scheme: leader sends PROPOSE, followers log and ACK, and on a quorum of ACKs the leader sends COMMIT; FIFO per-link ordering is leaned on via TCP). Zab's distinguishing guarantee is **primary order** (PO-atomic broadcast): transactions of a given primary are delivered in the order it issued them, and a new primary never reorders or interleaves an old primary's committed prefix — essential because ZooKeeper proposals are incremental state deltas, not idempotent commands. Structurally Zab is very close to Raft; the salient differences are explicit synchronization-phase state transfer versus Raft's incremental per-follower repair, and separate leader election versus election integrated into the consensus terms.

**Viewstamped Replication (VR).** VR (Oki & Liskov, 1988; "VR Revisited," Liskov & Cowling, 2012) predates Paxos's publication and is essentially the same algorithm in state-machine form. Configuration is a fixed set of 2f+1 replicas; the **view number** determines the primary deterministically (primary = view-number mod N), avoiding a distinct election protocol. In **normal operation**, the primary assigns each client request an op-number, sends PREPARE⟨view, op-number, request, commit-number⟩; backups append in op-number order and reply PREPARE-OK; on f PREPARE-OKs (f+1 counting itself) the primary executes, replies to the client, and piggybacks or sends COMMIT. A per-client **client table** provides at-most-once semantics by caching the latest request number and reply. On suspected primary failure, replicas run the **view change**: STARTVIEWCHANGE messages gather a quorum for view v+1, each participant sends DOVIEWCHANGE with its log, last-normal view, op-number, and commit-number to the new primary, which adopts the log with the largest ⟨last-normal-view, op-number⟩ — guaranteeing committed operations survive, the analogue of Raft's up-to-date rule performed by log transfer rather than vote filtering — and announces STARTVIEW. VR Revisited adds a **recovery protocol** (a rejoining replica uses a nonce and a quorum of RECOVERY-RESPONSEs to rebuild state, enabling diskless operation), state transfer, and a reconfiguration protocol driven through the log.

**Virtual synchrony / ISIS.** The virtual synchrony model (Birman & Joseph, ISIS toolkit) organizes processes into **process groups** with explicit membership **views**. Its core guarantee is that view changes are totally ordered relative to message deliveries: all surviving members deliver the same set of messages in the same view ("same view delivery"), so a multicast is received by exactly the membership that the sender observed. A **flush protocol** stabilizes in-flight messages before a new view is installed, and the gbcast primitive orders membership changes themselves. ISIS layered ordering disciplines over this: **CBCAST** (causal order via vector timestamps), **ABCAST** (total order, classically via a token or sequencer), and FBCAST (FIFO). Failure handling differs philosophically from quorum consensus: a suspected process is *excluded from the view* (and must rejoin via state transfer), trading possible false exclusions for fast reconfiguration — the lineage behind modern group-communication systems (Horus, Spread, JGroups) and primary-partition replication.

**Kafka replication and KRaft.** Classic Kafka replicates each partition through a leader and an **in-sync replica (ISR)** set. Followers pull records from the leader; the leader advances the **high watermark** to the minimum log end offset replicated across the ISR, and only records below it are readable by consumers. A producer with acks=all is acknowledged once all current ISR members have the record; the controller shrinks the ISR when followers lag (replica.lag.time.max.ms), so the effective commit quorum is dynamic rather than a fixed majority — f failures are tolerated with f+1 ISR members, at the cost of durability depending on min.insync.replicas and the **unclean leader election** setting (electing a non-ISR replica trades consistency for availability). **Leader epochs** (KIP-101) replace high-watermark-based truncation: a follower asks the new leader for the end offset of its last epoch and truncates divergent suffixes exactly, fixing data-loss and divergence anomalies — directly analogous to Raft's term-based log repair. **KRaft** (KIP-500) replaces the ZooKeeper-based controller with a Raft-variant quorum replicating the metadata log; its notable deviation from standard Raft is **pull-based replication** — followers fetch from the leader, reusing Kafka's fetch protocol, with the fetch itself conveying follower progress and serving the role of AppendEntries responses — plus standard Raft term/vote semantics for controller election. Brokers then replay the metadata log as observers, making cluster metadata itself an application of the replicated log.

A unifying remark for synthesis: Raft, Multi-Paxos, Zab, and VR are best viewed as one design family — leader-based total-order broadcast with majority (or, per FPaxos, merely intersecting) quorums, differing in how leader legitimacy is established (vote filtering on log recency vs. log transfer to the new leader), how logs are repaired, and how reconfiguration enters the log — while EPaxos and virtual synchrony represent the genuinely different points in the design space (leaderless dependency ordering, and membership-view-based delivery guarantees, respectively).

# Area 4: Lease-Based Coordination

## Gray–Cheriton Leases

The lease abstraction originates with Cary Gray and David Cheriton (SOSP 1989), who introduced it as a fault-tolerant mechanism for distributed file cache consistency. A lease is a contract granting its holder a right (originally: the right to serve reads from a cache, with a guarantee of invalidation before conflicting writes) for a bounded term. The crucial property distinguishing a lease from a lock is that it expires: if the holder crashes or becomes unreachable, the grantor regains the right unilaterally once the term elapses, so no recovery protocol is needed to break a dead holder's claim.

Correctness does not require synchronized clocks, only bounded clock drift rate: if the grantor and holder measure durations with clocks whose rates differ by at most a known factor ε, the holder can conservatively treat its lease as expired slightly earlier than the grantor does. The grantor, before performing an action that conflicts with an outstanding lease, must either receive an explicit relinquishment/acknowledgment from the holder or wait out the full term. The central engineering tradeoff Gray and Cheriton quantified: short terms minimize the write-blocking window after a holder failure, while long terms amortize renewal traffic and tolerate transient network hiccups; renewal is cheap because a renewal message can be piggybacked and because leases are typically renewed well before expiry. The same analysis underlies essentially every modern lease: leader leases in Raft implementations (for serving linearizable reads locally), master leases in Chubby, and leader leases in Spanner.

Two failure modes shape all later designs. First, a paused holder (long GC pause, VM migration, network partition) may believe its lease is valid after the grantor has expired it and re-granted — the "stale leaseholder" problem, which motivates fencing (below). Second, the grantor itself must be fault-tolerant, which is why production lease services (Chubby, ZooKeeper, etcd) are built atop a consensus-replicated state machine.

## Chubby: Coarse-Grained Advisory Locks and Sequencers

Chubby (Mike Burrows, OSDI 2006) is Google's lock service: a cell of five replicas running Multi-Paxos, electing a master that holds a master lease; clients speak only to the master. Chubby deliberately targets coarse-grained locking — locks held for hours or days (e.g., GFS master election, Bigtable tablet-server membership) — because coarse-grained use makes lock-service availability, not throughput, the binding constraint, and it survives brief Chubby outages.

Key mechanisms:

**Sessions and KeepAlives.** A client maintains a session with the master via periodic KeepAlive RPCs; the master responds by extending the session lease. KeepAlives are also the channel for event notifications and cache invalidations (the master blocks the KeepAlive reply to deliver them, keeping all master-to-client traffic on one RPC pattern, which plays well with firewalls). If a client's session lease expires at the client, the session enters "jeopardy"; the client gets a grace period (~45s) to reconnect to a new master before the session is declared expired, at which point its locks and ephemeral files are released.

**Advisory locks.** Chubby locks are advisory, not mandatory: holding the lock on a file confers no protection on the file's data; cooperating processes must check the lock by convention. Burrows argues mandatory locks add little, because protected resources usually live in other services anyway.

**Lock-delay.** If a lock holder fails (rather than cleanly releasing), Chubby can keep the lock unavailable for a configurable lock-delay (up to a minute), reducing the window in which a stale holder and a new holder act concurrently. This is a probabilistic mitigation, not a guarantee.

**Sequencers.** The guaranteed mechanism. On acquiring a lock, a client may request a sequencer: an opaque byte string naming the lock, its mode, and its lock generation number (incremented on each acquisition). The client passes the sequencer along with requests to downstream servers (e.g., a Bigtable server presenting it to GFS); the downstream server validates it against Chubby (or a cached validity window) and rejects requests bearing a stale generation. This is exactly the fencing-token pattern, with Chubby's lock generation number serving as the monotonic token.

## ZooKeeper: Ephemeral Nodes and Sessions

ZooKeeper (Hunt, Konar, Junqueira, Reed, USENIX ATC 2010) deliberately exposes a lower-level API than Chubby — a hierarchical namespace of znodes with watches — and lets clients build coordination recipes. Replication uses Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast), a primary-backup atomic broadcast protocol; every state change carries a zxid, a 64-bit identifier whose high 32 bits are the epoch and low 32 bits a counter, totally ordering all updates.

**Sessions.** A client session has a negotiated timeout; the client sends heartbeats, and the session migrates transparently across server failovers. If the ensemble receives nothing within the timeout, the session is expired by the leader.

**Ephemeral znodes.** A znode created with the EPHEMERAL flag is automatically deleted when its creating session expires or closes. This ties liveness of data to liveness of a client, giving group membership almost for free: each member creates an ephemeral znode under a group directory; watchers on the directory learn of joins and (after session timeout) failures. The SEQUENTIAL flag appends a monotonically increasing counter to the znode name, assigned under Zab's total order.

**Lock recipe and the herd effect.** The standard exclusive-lock recipe: create an ephemeral sequential znode under `/lock`; if yours has the lowest sequence number you hold the lock; otherwise set a watch on the znode with the next-lower sequence number and wait. Watching only the predecessor (rather than everyone watching the lock directory) avoids the herd effect, where a single release wakes all waiters and triggers O(n) notifications and retries.

**The fencing gap.** ZooKeeper's session machinery alone does not make a "lock" safe against stale holders: a client whose session has expired may not learn this before performing one more side-effecting action. The correct pattern is to use a monotonic value that the ZooKeeper ensemble itself ordered — the czxid (creation zxid) or the sequence number of the lock znode — as a fencing token presented to the protected resource. ZooKeeper provides the token material; the resource must enforce it.

## Fencing Tokens

The general mechanism, articulated sharply in Martin Kleppmann's 2016 analysis of Redis's Redlock ("How to do distributed locking") and in *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*: no lease/lock protocol relying on elapsed time can alone prevent a stale holder from acting, because the holder can be arbitrarily delayed between checking its lease and issuing its write (GC pause, page fault, network queuing). The fix moves the safety check to the protected resource. The lock service issues, with each grant, a fencing token — a number that strictly increases across successive grants of the same lock (Chubby's generation number, a ZooKeeper zxid/sequence number, Raft term, an etcd revision). Every request to the protected resource carries the token, and the resource rejects any request whose token is lower than the highest it has already seen. A stale holder's writes, arriving with an old token after a newer grant has touched the resource, are refused. The requirement this imposes — the storage/resource layer must be able to perform the monotonicity check atomically with the operation — is the practical limitation: fencing works for a database or a versioned object store, but not for a resource with no conditional-write capability. Kleppmann's specific complaint about Redlock is that it issues no such token and depends on timing assumptions (bounded clock drift across independent Redis masters, bounded pauses) that fail exactly in the scenarios locks exist to guard, making it unsafe for correctness-critical mutual exclusion (acceptable only for efficiency-oriented locking, where a violated lock wastes work rather than corrupting data).

## Clock-Bound Leases: Spanner Leader Leases with TrueTime

Spanner (Corbett et al., OSDI 2012) shows how explicitly bounded clock uncertainty converts leases from a heuristic into a provable invariant. TrueTime exposes `TT.now()` as an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain absolute time, with uncertainty ε kept to a few milliseconds by GPS and atomic-clock time masters.

Each Paxos group elects a leader that acquires a leader lease (default 10 seconds) by collecting lease votes from a quorum of replicas; the lease is extended implicitly on successful writes. The enforced **disjointness invariant**: for each Paxos group, the lease intervals of successive leaders are disjoint in absolute time — at most one leader can believe itself leaseholder at any instant. This is achievable precisely because TrueTime bounds uncertainty: a replica granting a lease vote promises not to vote again until `TT.after(lease_end)` is true by its own interval; a leader considers its lease expired once `TT.after(its lease votes' minimum end)` holds; a candidate leader waits out the previous lease conservatively using interval endpoints. A departing leader must also respect the timestamps it has promised: before abdicating it waits until `TT.after(s_max)`, where s_max is the maximum timestamp it has assigned, so the next leader cannot assign a smaller timestamp.

The payoff is twofold. First, single-leader invariants (monotonically increasing Paxos write timestamps within a group) hold in absolute time, which Spanner's external-consistency argument (Area 6) depends on. Second, the leaseholder can serve strongly consistent reads at timestamps below its safe time without a round of consensus, because disjointness rules out a rival leader having committed anything it hasn't seen. The contrast with Gray–Cheriton is instructive: classic leases assume only bounded drift rate and gain safety by conservative waiting of unknown real-time extent; TrueTime leases buy tight, measured bounds with hardware, so the waiting is short and the disjointness guarantee is exact.

---

# Area 5: Membership Changes

The core hazard in reconfiguring a consensus group is always the same: during a transition, if the old configuration C_old and the new configuration C_new can each independently form a quorum, two leaders can be elected and two different values committed for the same slot — a split brain created not by partition but by the configuration change itself. Every mechanism below is a different way of ensuring the quorums of any two concurrently active configurations intersect.

## Raft Joint Consensus (C_old,new)

In the original Raft paper (Ongaro & Ousterhout, USENIX ATC 2014), arbitrary configuration changes go through a transitional joint configuration C_old,new. The protocol has two phases, each an ordinary log entry:

The leader first appends a C_old,new entry. While in joint consensus, elections and entry commitment require **separate majorities from both** C_old and C_new (not a majority of the union). This is the intersection guarantee: no quorum of C_old alone and no quorum of C_new alone can act unilaterally during the transition. Once C_old,new is committed, the leader appends a C_new entry; once that commits, the transition is complete and servers outside C_new shut down.

Two subtleties are easy to get wrong. First, a server adopts a configuration **as soon as the entry is appended to its log**, not when committed — necessary because otherwise configuration entries would have to be committed under a configuration they're changing, creating a circularity; the cost is that a configuration entry can be truncated, requiring servers to fall back to the previous configuration in their log. Second, three practical issues the paper addresses: new servers join as non-voting learners to catch up before counting toward quorums (else availability dips while they replicate a long log); a leader not in C_new continues leading until C_new commits, then steps down (it manages a quorum excluding itself, not counting itself in majorities); and removed servers, no longer receiving heartbeats, will time out and start elections that disrupt the live cluster — mitigated by the PreVote-style rule that servers ignore RequestVote RPCs received within the minimum election timeout of hearing from a current leader.

## Single-Server Changes, the 2015 Bug, and Its Fix

Ongaro's dissertation (2014) proposed a simpler scheme now used by most Raft implementations (etcd, HashiCorp Raft): permit only one server to be added or removed per configuration change. The safety argument: a majority of C_old and a majority of C_new necessarily overlap when the configurations differ by one member, so no transitional joint phase is needed — each change is a single log entry, and quorums are computed against the latest configuration entry in the log.

In July 2015, Ongaro reported on the raft-dev mailing list a bug in this scheme as described in the dissertation. The problem arises when membership changes race with leader changes: a leader in term T appends configuration D₁ (not yet committed); it is deposed; a new leader elected under an older configuration (because D₁ wasn't replicated to it) appends a *different* single-server change D₂. D₁ and D₂ each differ from the base configuration by one server, so each overlaps the base — but D₁ and D₂ may **not overlap each other**, and disjoint majorities can then commit conflicting entries, violating the fundamental safety property.

**The fix**: a leader may not append a configuration-change entry until it has committed an entry from its own current term (in practice, the no-op entry every new Raft leader appends on election). Committing a current-term entry forces a quorum of the current configuration to adopt the leader's log prefix, which ensures any earlier uncommitted configuration entry (like D₁) is either committed (and thus the new change builds on it) or overwritten before a new change can be proposed. Joint consensus as described in the published paper does not suffer this particular bug, though implementations of it have their own pitfalls.

## Paxos Reconfiguration: the α Parameter and Stop Commands

Lamport's classic prescription ("Paxos Made Simple," 2001; elaborated in "Reconfiguring a State Machine," Lamport, Malkhi & Zhou, 2010) treats the configuration as part of the replicated state: the configuration used to execute consensus instance i+α is determined by the state after applying command i. The parameter α bounds the pipeline: at most α instances may be in flight concurrently, because the configuration of instance i+α is unknown until instance i is chosen. With α = 1 the system is fully serial; large α gives pipelining but delays the effect of a reconfiguration by α commands (implementations pad with no-ops to make a change take effect promptly — MultiPaxos deployments like Chubby's underlying layer use variants of this).

The same paper surveys alternatives that decouple reconfiguration from the α window, notably **stoppable state machines / stop commands** (building on "Stoppable Paxos," Lamport, Malkhi, Zhou 2008): a distinguished *stop* command is the final command of the current configuration's state machine; once a stop is chosen at instance i, no command can be chosen after i in that configuration, and a new state machine (new configuration, logically a fresh sequence of instances) is started, initialized from the old machine's final state. This cleanly serializes "old epoch ends, new epoch begins," at the cost of a brief unavailability window while the handoff occurs. **Vertical Paxos** (Lamport, Malkhi, Zhou, PODC 2009) is the related technique of changing configuration *per ballot* rather than per instance, with an external auxiliary master (itself possibly a small Paxos group, e.g., a Chubby-like service) authorizing each new ballot's configuration; read and write quorums can then differ per ballot, and new configurations must read state across the previous ballot's quorum before activating.

## Viewstamped Replication: View Changes versus Reconfiguration

Viewstamped Replication (Oki & Liskov, PODC 1988; "Viewstamped Replication Revisited," Liskov & Cowling, MIT TR 2012) makes a distinction worth keeping sharp, because the two mechanisms are often conflated.

A **view change** replaces the primary *within a fixed membership*. Views are numbered; the primary of view v is determined deterministically (round-robin by replica index in VR Revisited). When replicas suspect the primary (missed commits/heartbeats), they send StartViewChange for view v+1; upon a quorum, each sends DoViewChange to the new primary, carrying its log, its last normal view, and its op-number; the new primary selects the most up-to-date log among a quorum of DoViewChange messages (choosing by largest last-normal-view, then largest op-number — the analogue of Raft's up-to-date voting rule, done by state transfer rather than vote restriction) and announces StartView. View changes are the *failover* mechanism, analogous to Raft terms/elections and to Multi-Paxos ballot changes; membership is untouched.

**Reconfiguration** (Section 7 of VR Revisited) changes the replica set itself and is driven through the normal case as a special client request: an administrator submits a *reconfiguration request*, the primary commits it in the current group like any operation but stops accepting further client requests at that op-number; epochs (epoch numbers, incremented per configuration) delimit configurations. The new group runs a state-transfer protocol to fetch the committed state from old-group members; old replicas remain alive, read-only for state transfer, until the new epoch's quorum is up to date, then shut down. Replicas receiving messages from an older epoch inform the sender of the new configuration. The design is essentially the "commit a final command, then hand off" shape — kin to stop commands — embedded in VR's primary-backup framework.

## Dynamic Quorum Adjustment and Flexible Quorums

The classical requirement — all quorums are majorities of a fixed set — is one point in a design space. **Flexible Paxos** (Howard, Malkhi & Spiegelman, OPODIS 2016) proved that Paxos needs only that *phase-1 (leader-election) quorums intersect phase-2 (replication) quorums*; two phase-2 quorums need not intersect each other. This permits, e.g., in a group of n, replication quorums of size n−f with election quorums of size f+1, trading rare-election cost for cheap steady-state commits, and permits grid quorums. The same relaxation applies to Raft (FPaxos-style Raft variants require only that election quorums intersect replication quorums), and it reframes reconfiguration: a configuration change is safe exactly when the new configuration's election quorums intersect all replication quorums through which uncommitted-but-committable state may have passed.

Related dynamic-quorum mechanisms in production systems include **witness/arbiter replicas** (non-data-bearing voters that participate in quorums to break ties cheaply — used in VR-style and Paxos deployments), **learner/non-voting stages** during member addition (etcd learners, Raft catch-up phase) that keep quorum size stable while a replica catches up, and **quorum leases** (Moraru, Andersen, Kaminsky, SoCC 2014), which grant read leases to a designated subset of replicas so reads are served locally while writes synchronously update all leaseholders — a lease-shaped quorum adjustment connecting back to Area 4. The historical root is dynamic voting / quorum adjustment in replicated databases (Jajodia & Mutchler; Davčev & Burkhard, 1980s), where the quorum basis shrinks to the majority of the *previously current* partition to preserve one distinguished lineage of state — the same intersection-across-time reasoning consensus reconfiguration formalizes.

---

# Area 6: Consistency Models

Consistency models are contracts constraining which orderings of operations a system may expose. The useful organizing axes: does the model respect *real time* (operations by different clients ordered by actual non-overlap), does it respect *program/session order*, does it respect *causality*, and is it *composable* across objects.

## Linearizability

Defined by Herlihy and Wing (TOPLAS 1990). An execution is linearizable if each operation appears to take effect atomically at some *linearization point* between its invocation and its response, and the resulting total order is legal for the object's sequential specification. The defining obligation is the **real-time constraint**: if operation A completes before operation B begins (in wall-clock terms, across any clients), A precedes B in the linearization. Consequences: reads always observe the latest completed write (recency), and linearizability is **compositional (a local property)** — a history over multiple objects is linearizable iff its per-object projections are — which is what lets you reason about a system of linearizable registers object by object. It is also *non-blocking* as a correctness condition (a pending total operation never must wait for another to complete to preserve the property), distinguishing it from strict serializability's transactional setting: linearizability is the single-operation/single-object specialization; strict serializability extends the same real-time requirement to multi-object transactions. Cost: the CAP theorem (Gilbert & Lynch's formalization of Brewer) shows a linearizable register cannot remain available under partition, and even partition-free latency is lower-bounded (Attiya–Welch). Systems providing it: a Raft/Multi-Paxos state machine with reads through the leader's lease or via ReadIndex, Spanner (and beyond — see external consistency), etcd linearizable reads, ZooKeeper *writes* (reads are only sequentially consistent unless preceded by `sync`).

## Sequential Consistency

Lamport (IEEE ToC, 1979): an execution is sequentially consistent if there exists a single total order of all operations, consistent with each individual process's **program order**, under which every read returns the value of the most recent write. The difference from linearizability is exactly the dropped real-time constraint: a client may observe arbitrarily stale state, provided everyone observes writes in one agreed order and no one's own operations are reordered. Sequential consistency is **not compositional**: two objects each sequentially consistent can interleave into a non-sequentially-consistent whole (the standard two-queue counterexample in Herlihy & Wing), which is why it is a pleasant *memory model* for a single shared-memory machine but an awkward distributed contract. ZooKeeper's default client view is a practical instance: all updates are totally ordered by Zab, each client sees them in order, but a read served by a lagging follower may be stale — "sequential, not linearizable." In multiprocessor terms, this is the model against which hardware memory models (TSO, ARM's weaker orders) are defined as relaxations.

## Causal Consistency and Causal+

Causal consistency requires that operations related by **potential causality** — Lamport's happens-before relation (program order, reads-from, and transitive closure; "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events," CACM 1978) — be observed in that order by every client; concurrent (causally unrelated) writes may be seen in different orders by different replicas. It is the strongest model implementable with full availability and partition tolerance in an always-available, convergent setting (Mahajan, Alvisi, Dahlin's result on real-time causal consistency), which makes it the natural ceiling for geo-replicated "ALPS" systems (Availability, low Latency, Partition-tolerance, Scalability). Implementations track causality with **vector clocks** or more compact dependency metadata: **COPS** (Lloyd, Freedman, Kaminsky, Andersen, SOSP 2011) introduced **causal+ consistency** — causal consistency plus *convergent conflict handling*, meaning causally concurrent writes to the same key are resolved identically at all replicas (by last-writer-wins or an application merge), so replicas don't diverge forever on conflicts. COPS attaches explicit dependencies to each write and a remote datacenter applies a write only after its dependencies are locally visible; its successor Eiger extended this to column-family data and read/write-only transactions; bolt-on causal consistency (Bailis et al.) layers the same guarantee over an eventually consistent store. The known cost is *dependency metadata and visibility latency* ("throughput collapse" under heavy fan-out of dependencies), the focus of later systems (Orbe, GentleRain with loosely synchronized physical clocks).

## Eventual Consistency

The weakest commonly named model (popularized by Vogels, CACM 2009; mechanized much earlier in Grapevine and in **Bayou**): if updates cease, replicas *eventually* converge to the same state; nothing is promised about intermediate reads — no recency, no ordering, no session guarantees. It is a pure **liveness/convergence** property, which is why it must be paired with an anti-entropy mechanism (gossip, Merkle-tree synchronization as in Dynamo, hinted handoff, read repair) and a **conflict-resolution policy**: last-writer-wins (with its silent-loss hazard under clock skew), application-level merge of **sibling** versions exposed via version vectors (Dynamo's vector-clock-tagged multivalue reads), or CRDTs, which make convergence automatic. Amazon Dynamo (DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007) is the canonical production statement: sloppy quorums (R + W tunable against N) plus anti-entropy, trading recency for availability and latency per the CAP/PACELC analysis (Abadi's PACELC adds the latency-vs-consistency tradeoff even absent partitions).

## CRDTs

Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero, Zawirski; "A comprehensive study of CRDTs," 2011) are data types whose replicas can be updated independently and merged deterministically, guaranteeing **strong eventual consistency (SEC)**: any two replicas that have delivered the same *set* of updates (in any order) are in the same state — convergence as a safety property, not just a liveness hope. Two standard formulations, provably equivalent in expressive power:

**State-based (CvRDT):** the state space forms a **join-semilattice**; updates are inflations (move monotonically up the lattice); replicas exchange full or delta states and merge with the **least upper bound (join)**, which is commutative, associative, and idempotent — so gossip over an unreliable, reordering, duplicating network converges. Delta-state CRDTs (Almeida, Shoker, Baquero) ship small join-irreducible deltas instead of full states.

**Operation-based (CmRDT):** replicas broadcast operations, which must be delivered exactly once in **causal order**, and *concurrent* operations must commute; the delivery requirement shifts burden onto a reliable causal broadcast layer.

Canonical constructions: **G-Counter** (vector of per-replica monotonic counts, join = pointwise max, value = sum) and **PN-Counter** (two G-Counters, increments minus decrements); **LWW-Register** (timestamped value, join = max timestamp, inheriting last-writer-wins's lost-update semantics); **G-Set** and **2P-Set** (add-only; add/remove-once); **OR-Set** (observed-remove set: adds tag elements with unique identifiers, removal deletes only *observed* tags, so a concurrent add wins over a remove — resolving the add/remove ambiguity that 2P-Set punts on); sequence CRDTs for collaborative text (**RGA**, **Logoot/LSEQ**, **Treedoc**), the basis of Automerge and Yjs. The structural limitation: CRDTs guarantee convergence, not application invariants spanning the datatype (no "balance ≥ 0" without coordination); hybrid designs (RedBlue consistency, Indigo) classify operations into coordination-free and coordinated classes.

## Read-Your-Writes and Session Guarantees

Terry et al., "Session Guarantees for Weakly Consistent Replicated Data" (PDIS 1994, from the Bayou project) defined four per-**session** properties that make eventual consistency tolerable to a single client without imposing global order:

**Read-your-writes** (a read observes all prior writes of the same session), **monotonic reads** (successive reads never move backward — a later read reflects at least the writes any earlier read reflected), **monotonic writes** (a session's writes are applied everywhere in issue order), and **writes-follow-reads** (a write causally after a read is ordered after the writes that read observed, at all replicas — the session-local kernel of causality). Implementation in Bayou: the session manager carries two version-vector sets, a read-set and a write-set, and a replica may serve a session only if its state dominates the relevant vectors; practical systems implement the same idea with sticky sessions (pin a client to a replica), client-tracked low-water-mark timestamps/LSNs presented on each request (e.g., MongoDB causal sessions with cluster-time tokens, Azure Cosmos DB session consistency with session tokens), or read-after-write routing to the primary. Jointly, the four guarantees per session amount to causal consistency restricted to a single client's observations — the bridge between the eventual and causal tiers of the hierarchy.

## External Consistency in Spanner

External consistency (the term originates with David Gifford's 1982 thesis) is the strongest model on this list: the system behaves as a single machine executing transactions serially, in an order consistent with their **global wall-clock commit order** — if transaction T₁ commits (its commit completes) before T₂ starts, then T₁'s commit timestamp is smaller and T₂ observes T₁. For transactions this coincides with **strict serializability**; it is linearizability lifted to multi-object, multi-shard transactions across the entire database.

Spanner achieves it with TrueTime and two rules. **Timestamp assignment:** the coordinator leader assigns a committing transaction a timestamp s no less than `TT.now().latest` (and, within a Paxos group, greater than any previously assigned timestamp — guaranteed across leader changes by the lease disjointness and s_max handoff of Area 4). **Commit wait:** the leader delays acknowledging the commit and releasing locks until `TT.after(s)` is true — i.e., until s is guaranteed to be in the past at every node on Earth. The correctness argument is two inequalities: s₁ ≤ absolute-commit-time(T₁) (by commit wait) and absolute-start-time(T₂) ≤ s₂ (by the timestamp-assignment rule), so T₁'s completion preceding T₂'s start in real time forces s₁ < s₂. The expected wait is on the order of 2ε (ε being TrueTime's instantaneous uncertainty, kept to ~1–7 ms), overlapped with the Paxos commit round so it is often hidden. The same timestamp discipline yields **consistent snapshot reads**: any read at timestamp t, served by any replica whose *safe time* exceeds t, observes a globally consistent prefix, giving lock-free read-only transactions that are nonetheless externally consistent. The contrast with non-clock-based designs is the essential lesson: CockroachDB, with NTP-grade uncertainty, cannot afford commit-wait over large ε and instead provides serializability with per-key linearizability via uncertainty-interval restarts, illustrating precisely what the hardware clock investment in TrueTime purchases.

---

**Cross-cutting note for synthesis:** the three areas interlock. Fencing tokens are what make lease-based leadership *safe* rather than probabilistic, and the tokens themselves (terms, epochs, zxids, view numbers, ballot numbers) are the same monotonic epoch identifiers that membership-change protocols use to order configurations; external consistency is what a correctly leased, correctly reconfigured consensus system can promise upward to clients when clock uncertainty is bounded. Terminological cautions worth preserving: view change ≠ reconfiguration (VR), sequential ≠ linearizable (ZooKeeper reads), eventual consistency (liveness) ≠ strong eventual consistency (CRDT safety), and advisory locks + lock-delay (probabilistic) ≠ sequencers/fencing (guaranteed).
